messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ethan, a 39-year-old construction worker, still found himself haunted by the high-rise site where his life had irrevocably fractured two years prior. He had been supervising a crew, the smell of fresh concrete and damp earth thick in the air, when a structural beam, improperly secured, had given way. He watched, frozen, as his friend and colleague, Miguel, fell four stories. The image of Miguel’s hard hat tumbling ahead of him, the sickening thud, and the sudden, metallic taste of fear in Ethan’s mouth, all remained as vivid as the day it happened. He could still smell the coppery scent of blood mixing with the dust, a phantom odor that would ambush him without warning.

In the aftermath, Ethan struggled to reconcile what he had witnessed. His core "beliefs about how the world works," particularly his conviction that hard work and caution kept you safe, felt "completely destroyed." He had come to believe that "he couldn't stop bad things from happening to him," a gnawing sense of "helplessness" that spread through every aspect of his life. This profound sense of "inadequacy," the feeling that he was fundamentally unable to protect himself or others from the arbitrary cruelty of life, began to dictate his responses. It was as if these convictions acted as a magnet for the most horrifying images of the accident, ensuring they replayed in his mind with relentless intensity, always confirming his worst fears.

As these negative appraisals solidified, Ethan found himself turning to a series of coping mechanisms. Convinced of his inherent "inadequacy" and the world's capriciousness, he started to "gamble to distract myself or feel excitement," a desperate attempt to feel something other than dread, or perhaps to exert some control over an outcome, however fleeting. He also began to "suppress anger," fearing that any outward expression of strong emotion would only confirm his "helplessness" and make him even more vulnerable.

The sensory details of the accident continued to plague him. His memories of Miguel’s fall were mostly "pictures or images," flashing across his mind at unexpected moments. Sometimes, the "olfactory recall" would hit him mid-shift, the phantom scent of blood and concrete so potent it would make him gag, or the "taste vividness" of that metallic fear would return while he was eating lunch. These intrusive, visceral memories constantly reinforced his negative appraisals. Each time a memory returned, it brought with it the crushing certainty that "he couldn't stop bad things from happening to him," deepening his sense of "helplessness" and confirming that his "beliefs about how the world works had been completely destroyed."

The intensity of these memories, particularly the vivid "visual memories" and the jarring "olfactory recall," made Ethan desperate for escape. When the images became too overwhelming, he would "deliberately try to leave my body or blank out," detaching from the present moment until the internal cinema subsided. This deliberate dissociation became a frequent strategy on construction sites when the clang of metal or the sight of scaffolding would trigger a flashback. His gambling also escalated, an increasingly urgent way to drown out the constant replay of the accident, a maladaptive strategy fueled directly by the torment of his memories.

The cycle tightened. His deepening conviction of "inadequacy" and "helplessness" led him further into his maladaptive strategies, causing his marriage to crumble and contributing to his divorce. His ex-wife described him as emotionally absent, a consequence of his constant anger suppression and deliberate dissociation. His gambling debts mounted, reinforcing his sense of personal failure. On the job, he found himself increasingly withdrawn, his focus compromised by the constant threat of a memory ambush. He had come to believe that the world was inherently unsafe, and his own actions were futile against its harsh realities. He finally sought help, not sure if anything could truly change, but desperate to escape the tightening grip of a past he couldn't outrun and a future he felt powerless to shape.
